newsitem.title: JAPAN: NEC develops first 4-gigabit DRAM chip.
newsitem.headline: NEC develops first 4-gigabit DRAM chip.

text.p: Japanese electronics company NEC Corp. announced Thursday it had developed the world's first 4-gigait dynamic random access memory (DRAM) computer chip, the most sophisticated memory chip yet.
"It can store the complete works of William Shakespeare 64 times over," NEC Vice resident Hajime Sasaki told a news conference.

NEC, the world's second-largest memory chip maker after South Korea's Samsung Electronics Co., said it had beaten its Japanese, South Korean and American rivals in developing the state-of-the-art semiconductor.
A 4-gigabit DRAM, which is about four times the size of of a thumbnail, is capable of storing data equivalent to 16,000 newspaper pages. A gigabit is one billion bits.
DRAM chips are currently used mainly in personal computers.
Sasaki said NEC plans to send out sample shipments of the chip by the year 2000 and that it was seeking an early launch of the product.
NEC used technology in which the circuit lines on the chip have a width of only 0.15 micron. A micron is one-millionth of a metre.
The process has been confirmed by the global semiconductor body, the International Solid State Circuits Conference in the United Sates, Sasaki said.

NEC said the chip is suitable for multimedia devices because it can store 47 minutes of full-motion video and six hours of audio data -- a memory capacity almost equal to a compact disc read-only memory.
NEC expects the size of the chip to be reduced to about half the current size within two to three years, Sasaki said.
NEC and Japan's Hitachi Ltd. developed 1-gigabit DRAMs at almost the same time in 1995, an NEC spokesman said.

Commercial production of the 4-gigabit chips will not begin until after the turn of the century, however, as the current mainstay chip is still the 16-megabit (16-million-bit) DRAM chip, which, although much less sophisticated by comparison, can store the equivalent of up to 128 newspaper pages of information.
Demand for the next-generation 64-megabit DRAM chip is expected to peak in late 1998.
NEC's announcement came just two days after Hitachi, Mitsubishi Electric Corp. and Dallas-based Texas Instruments Inc. said they had agreed to jointly develop 1-gigabit DRAM chips.
